newsitem.title: USA: Problems are not over yet for Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Problems are not over yet for Gingrich.

text.p: A weakened House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich is holding on to power following his unprecedented punishment for ethics violations but further problems remain that could eventually topple him.

Shaken and divided Republicans hope that focusing on their legislative agenda will help them weather the storm raised by a scathing House ethics committee report and Tuesday's 395-28 vote to reprimand the speaker and impose a $300,000 penalty.

Republican Representative Charles Canady of Florida, who was sharply critical of Gingrich's misconduct at the time of the House vote, said the speaker could still play a key role in moving the Republican agenda forward. But he said: "Only time will tell how things will go. The speaker has been damaged."
As Gingrich's allies rallied to his support and prayed for no more surprises, the speaker faced three potential hurdles to remaining in office for the next two years.
First, he has to find a way to pay his $300,000 penalty that will not arouse a new furore just as the House begins what all sides hope will be a productive session.

Gingrich is on notice that he cannot expect to avoid personal pain by taking the money from his campaign warchest. He said on Thursday that attorneys were working on the payment problem and "it will be legal and ethical."

Second, Gingrich's admission that he violated ethics rules did not clear up all of the charges involving his use of GOPAC, the political action committee he once headed. Still to be dealt with by the ethics committee are charges filed by Democrats a year ago that Gingrich received gifts and illegal campaign contributions from GOPAC. The committee expanded its investigation last September to get more evidence.

Finally, the committee is making available to the Internal Revenue Service the mass of documents that it gathered during its two-year investigation into Gingrich's use of tax-free charitable funds in his "To Renew America" campaign.

The committee made no finding as to whether he used the money illegally for partisan political purposes but Gingrich admitted he should have sought legal advice on the question. An IRS investigation could have a different result on the question of possible violations of federal law.

Gingrich was virtually invisible as the House voted on the first reprimand for a sitting speaker in U.S. history. But by Thursday he was back in the public eye, appearing at a news conference following a party leaders' "retreat" in the Virginia countryside.
The ostensible purpose was to announce a date for a House vote on one of Republicans' most treasured initiatives, a constitutional amendment to balance the budget.

Gingrich refused to comment on the House reprimand vote, saying only that he would make a speech about it "at an appropriate time in the future." He plans to hold two "town hall" meetings in his Georgia district on Saturday.

Except for the informal attire -- Gingrich and others in the group wore brightly coloured casual shirts -- the scene was familiar: the speaker as visionary, flanked by his top lieutenants, talking about Medicare and the ravages of diabetes, urging voters to make their voices heard on the balanced budget amendment.

But his role in the House is already less dominant than it was two years ago when, as the architect of the Republican takeover, he seemed unstoppable. Now power is less centralized and committee chairmen have resumed a more traditional role.
